clue.text: Radio’s offering of news in musical format? It’ll do for the present

indicators.note: radio carries only sound, so what it offers is heard rather than seen, and spelling is set aside

blocks.note: a newspaper delivered as rap would be a rapping paper

explanation.surface: A radio station tries a quirky idea: reading out the news as a piece of music.
explanation.walkthrough: RAPPING PAPER and WRAPPING PAPER sound the same, since the W is silent. 'Present' looks like 'the current time', but it is a gift.
explanation.definitionFit: Gifts are covered in decorative sheets before being handed over, so this material serves a present's needs.

clue.text: Bereaved person needing suitable period to drop name

indicators.note: to drop something is to let it fall away, so a letter goes missing from the word

blocks.note: a window is a suitable period for doing something
N is the standard abbreviation for name

explanation.surface: A grieving person needs a decent interval before letting go of a married name.
explanation.walkthrough: Take the N out of WINDOW to leave WIDOW.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman whose husband has died has suffered a loss, so she is one kind of mourner.

clue.text: Amusing person caught appearing later in sale

indicators.note: something that appears later turns up further along, so the letter is lifted out and slotted back in further on

blocks.note: old-fashioned slang: an entertaining or mischievous person is 'a caution'
C is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for caught

explanation.surface: A comedian gets arrested but only shows up at a sale afterwards.
explanation.walkthrough: In CAUTION, move the opening C (caught) two places later to get AUCTION. 'A caution' is dated British slang for a person who makes you laugh.
explanation.definitionFit: Goods are sold to the highest bidder at one, so it is a particular kind of public selling event.

clue.text: Source of his support filling senior politician with stoic indifference

indicators.note: a source is where something starts, so only the opening letter of the word is taken
a filling goes inside something, so these letters sit within the outer word

blocks.note: a leg supports a table or chair

explanation.surface: A backer's money underpins a leading politician who stays calm and unmoved.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Support' suggests political backing, but it is the body part a table stands on.
explanation.definitionFit: Besides mucus, the word means calmness of temperament, an old sense from the four humours of medieval medicine.

clue.text: Like charities for 6, possibly, supported by royal

indicators.note: 'possibly' says the letters might be arranged some other way, so they are reordered
in a down entry, whatever supports something sits under it, so this piece follows at the bottom

explanation.surface: Charitable organisations seem to be described as working for a soldier, with royal patronage.
explanation.walkthrough: FOR together with POINT MAN, the answer to 6, is rearranged; KING goes underneath.
explanation.definitionFit: Charities exist for a cause rather than to earn money for owners, which is exactly this business status.

clue.text: Redrawn Sunlit Hour with Cupid - beautiful

indicators.note: a picture that is redrawn is made again differently, so the letters get a new arrangement

explanation.surface: An artist repaints a lovely scene titled Sunlit Hour with Cupid.
explanation.walkthrough: The italics make the words look like a painting's title; they are the letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Pulchritude is a formal, rather comic word for physical loveliness, so this adjective simply means good-looking.

clue.text: Hint army’s lacking rearguard and lead soldier

indicators.note: a rearguard protects the back, so without it the last letter is lost

blocks.note: an army of things is a great many of them

explanation.surface: Someone suggests the army has no one guarding its rear and needs a soldier to lead.
explanation.walkthrough: MANY loses its last letter to give MAN. 'Rearguard' is a military word in the surface but just means the end letter.
explanation.definitionFit: On patrol, this soldier walks at the front of the unit, exposed first to danger.

clue.text: Underground material greeting last character entering European city

indicators.note: to enter is to go inside, so these letters go within the outer word

blocks.note: Z is the last letter of the alphabet

explanation.surface: A greeting and a final letter are scrawled on something buried beneath a European city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Last character' means the final letter of the alphabet, not of any word in the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a plant stem that grows horizontally beneath the soil, sending out roots and shoots, as ginger and irises do.

clue.text: Murderer showing nerve for an American engaged in a crime

indicators.note: to be engaged in something is to be caught up inside it, so one piece goes within another

blocks.note: 'a' plus SIN, a crime or wrong
sass is American slang for cheek or impudence

explanation.surface: A killer displays nerve on behalf of an American caught up in a crime.
explanation.walkthrough: SASS goes inside A SIN, after the S.
explanation.definitionFit: This is someone who kills an important person, typically for political reasons or for payment.

clue.text: Transaction securing Chrysler’s foremost car accessory

indicators.note: foremost means at the very front, so only the opening letter is used
to secure something is to hold it fast, so one piece holds another inside

blocks.note: a deal is a business transaction

explanation.surface: A business deal wins a leading car accessory contract for the carmaker Chrysler.
explanation.walkthrough: C goes inside DEAL.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a decorative sticker or transfer, often applied to a car's bodywork or window, the American term for one.

clue.text: Cancels dancing in full and finishes cancelling start of dancing

indicators.note: dancing letters move about and swap places, so they end up in another order
the start is where a word begins, so only its opening letter counts
cancelling something removes it, so that letter is struck out

blocks.note: to die is to finish or come to an end

explanation.surface: Someone calls off dancing completely and ends it by scrapping the start of the dance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dancing' appears twice: the first rearranges IN FULL, the second supplies D, which is removed from DIES.
explanation.definitionFit: To make something legally void or of no effect is to cancel it, the same verb in the same tense.

clue.text: Kitchen item that’s presented with an identical example

blocks.note: W is an abbreviation for with
a (dead) ringer is an exact likeness

explanation.surface: A kitchen gadget comes packaged along with a duplicate of itself.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dead ringer' means someone or something that looks exactly like another.
explanation.definitionFit: A mangle with rollers for squeezing water from washed laundry, traditionally kept in a kitchen or scullery.

clue.text: Physical discipline, very popular? Past year shows regression

indicators.note: regression is going backwards, so the letters are read from the far end

blocks.note: a hot item is very popular
Y is the abbreviation for year

explanation.surface: A fashionable exercise craze seems to have gone backwards over the last year.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark ends the definition and the first piece; 'shows regression' applies only to the past-and-year pair.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a form of exercise practised in a heated studio, and yoga is a system of bodily and mental training.

clue.text: Long fifth option at the ATM?

indicators.note: 'at' means located next to, so one piece sits beside the other

blocks.note: a cash machine asks for your personal identification number
in a multiple-choice list A to E, the fifth option is E

explanation.surface: Someone at a cash machine scrolls through the menu to a fifth choice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Long' looks like an adjective, but it is the verb meaning to yearn.
explanation.definitionFit: To yearn or ache for something is to long for it, both verbs of wistful desire.

clue.text: Many a hitch with this attitude to unions?

definitions.text: Many a hitch with this attitude to unions?

blocks.note: surface: lots of snags or problems
setter's reading: getting hitched means marrying, so many hitches are many marriages at once, and unions are marriages, not trade unions

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests industrial relations troubles; 'hitch' is slang for marriage and 'unions' are marriages.
explanation.definitionFit: The practice of having several spouses at the same time amounts to getting hitched repeatedly.

clue.text: Freak rains excited Cape Town residents?

indicators.note: excited things are stirred up and agitated, so the letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: Unusual downpours have the people of Cape Town worked up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Freak' looks like the anagram signal, but it is part of the letters; 'excited' does the stirring. The question mark admits that not every Cape Town resident fits.
explanation.definitionFit: These are Afrikaans-speaking South Africans of mainly Dutch descent, and many live in and around the Western Cape city.

clue.text: Love it, going climbing in county, returning again and again?

definitions.note: a verb phrase describing the behaviour; the answer is the noun for it

indicators.note: in a down entry, climbing means moving upwards, so the letters read from bottom to top
'in' places one thing inside another

blocks.note: love is zero in tennis, shaped like O
Devon is a county in south-west England

explanation.surface: A walker so loves hill-climbing in one county that they keep going back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Love' wants to be the definition, but it is the tennis zero that the wordplay needs. The definition is the whimsical last phrase, marked by the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: Deep loyalty and dedication show in repeated, faithful visits, the kind of commitment a fan or worshipper keeps up.

clue.text: Stop holding it, miss

indicators.note: to hold something is to have it within your grip, so one piece encloses another

blocks.note: a two-word phrasal verb meaning to omit, split open to hold the other piece

explanation.surface: Someone tells a young woman to stop gripping something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Miss' looks like a young woman; it is the verb to omit. 'Leave it out!' is British slang for 'stop it!'
explanation.definitionFit: In informal British speech this exclamation tells someone to quit what they are doing or saying.

clue.text: A term of respect encountered around large compound

indicators.note: to be found around something is to surround it, so one piece is wrapped round another

blocks.note: ma'am, a polite form of address
lg is an abbreviation for large

explanation.surface: A polite form of address is found surrounding a sizeable chemical substance.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe in ma'am drops out, as punctuation always does in crosswords.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a blend or mixture, especially an alloy of mercury with another metal, as used in dental fillings.

clue.text: A volume about what’s retained by banks?

blocks.note: V is the symbol for volume
on means about, as in a talk on a subject

explanation.surface: A book about the money banks keep in their reserves.
explanation.walkthrough: The banks are not financial but riverbanks: a river is held in by its banks.
explanation.definitionFit: The Avon is an English river, the one flowing through Stratford, and riverbanks contain its water.

clue.text: Dizzy sensation to check one attempt? That’s about right

indicators.note: 'about' means surrounding, so the earlier letters are placed round this one

blocks.note: I is the Roman numeral one
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A dizzy spell needs checking before one tries again, and that seems sensible.
explanation.walkthrough: 'That's about right' sounds like approval, but it tells you to put the letter for right inside the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a feeling that the surroundings are spinning, often linked with fear of heights.

clue.text: Red wind instrument’s not popular

indicators.note: 'not' excludes something, so those letters are taken away

explanation.surface: A red clarinet is not selling well.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove IN from CLARINET.
explanation.definitionFit: Claret is the British name for red Bordeaux wine, and hence also a deep purplish-red colour.

clue.text: Hurried in attempt to get to US city for its breakfast cereal

indicators.note: 'in' places one piece inside another
arriving next to something, so one piece follows directly after the other

explanation.surface: Someone rushes to reach an American city for its famous breakfast food.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hurried' comes first in the clue, but its letters sit inside the attempt, not before it.
explanation.definitionFit: A crunchy mix of toasted oats, nuts and dried fruit, eaten with milk or yoghurt in the morning.

clue.text: Crude advert, first to last, by Communist

indicators.note: the leading letter is sent to the back, rotating the word

blocks.note: a bill is a poster advertisement

explanation.surface: A tasteless poster campaign, start to finish, produced by a Communist.
explanation.walkthrough: Move the B of BILL to the end to get ILLB, then add RED.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone badly brought up shows rude, coarse manners, so both adjectives describe a lack of refinement.

clue.text: Medic heading off manager’s nonsense

indicators.note: with its head off, a word loses its first letter

explanation.surface: A doctor walks out on the manager's rubbish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heading off' reads as the medic leaving, but it beheads the next word.
explanation.definitionFit: Dross is waste scum on molten metal and so figuratively worthless rubbish or rot.

clue.text: Grandee having note provided in marvellous opening of opera

indicators.note: 'in' places one piece inside another
an opening is where a word begins, so its first letter is taken

explanation.surface: A nobleman has a letter delivered at the wonderful first night of an opera.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Note' suggests a message or a musical tone, but it is just its abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: Originally a Venetian magnate, the word is used for any person of high rank or great importance.

clue.text: Money putting an end to tender hearts in love

indicators.note: an end is where a word finishes, so its final letter is kept

blocks.note: H is the abbreviation for the card suit
love is zero in tennis, shaped like O

explanation.surface: Cash brings romance between tender-hearted lovers to a close.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tender' looks like soft; it is just the word whose end is taken. Rhino is old British slang for money.
explanation.definitionFit: Rhino is dated British slang for cash, like dosh or readies.

clue.text: Unusual living arrangements easier amongst freaks

indicators.note: to freak is to go wild, so the letters are thrown into disorder

explanation.surface: Odd household set-ups are simpler among unconventional people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Amongst' reads as a positional word, but it is fodder; 'freaks' is a verb here, not the people.
explanation.definitionFit: These are households of three people in a sexual relationship, a French phrase meaning household of three.
